content.text:
I would start with **declaration identity resolution**. Its central promise is consequential and precise: a resolved identity must never contain observations with different accepted source company numbers, including observations connected indirectly through records without a company number. A broken merge could attribute funding to the wrong organisation.

The [resolver]( /Users/jamie/development/exposed/exposed/src/lib/domain/models/declaration_resolution/identity.rs:257) already defends that promise in two ways. It identifies unanchored components with competing company attachments, then checks company numbers across the entire proposed component before joining it. That combination makes the transitive cases especially interesting. Imagine company 1 linking to an unknown observation, which also links to company 2. This is a proposed verification scenario, not a bug I found.

There are three credible starting areas:

| Target | Property to check | Why choose it |
|---|---|---|
| Identity resolution | No resolved identity contains conflicting source company numbers | Direct attribution harm; indirect links create combinations that examples can miss |
| Declaration loading | Concurrent loads and interrupted retries preserve atomic publication and monotonic state | Strong fit for exploring writer interleavings, crashes and retries |
| Funder display grouping | Groups are exactly connected components, use the minimum UUID, and retain only direct evidence | Clear graph contract with a compact, tractable input space |

Identity resolution is distinct from the later [funder display grouping](/Users/jamie/development/exposed/exposed/src/lib/domain/models/funder_grouping.rs:169). I would keep the first skill narrowly about identity, rather than combining both algorithms. Declared totals are also consequential, but their existing examples already cover substantial boundary, precision, null, zero, negative and foreign-currency behavior.

For identity resolution, **Kani would be my first tool candidate**, because it runs proof harnesses against Rust code. Dependency compatibility with this application still needs checking. Its bounded proofs require an explicit scope, so a reasonable initial experiment would use four observations and two distinct company-number tokens, varying eligible links, unknowns, entity kinds and observation ordering. That would establish a finite-domain result; it would not prove arbitrary strings or the upstream matching scores. See [Kani usage](https://model-checking.github.io/kani/usage.html) and [loop bounds](https://model-checking.github.io/kani/tutorial-loop-unwinding.html).

For loading, I would instead use TLA+ with two writers, two declarations, crashes and retries. [TLC checks invariants over finite models](https://nightly.tlapl.us/doc/model/overview-page.html). The model would assume PostgreSQL transaction atomicity and writers respecting the advisory lock. An exact retry intentionally refreshes the group projection, so “retry changes nothing anywhere” would be the wrong property.

Following the skill’s “prove it works” requirement, eventual delivery should demonstrate that removing a real Rust safeguard makes the check fail, then restore it. A passing handwritten mirror would provide weaker evidence.

No proofs have run, and these findings do not establish a bug. Would you prefer to begin with attribution correctness in identity resolution, or interruption and concurrency safety in loading?
